title: Left for Dead on Everest: The Full Case of Beck Weathers
description:
Case 014. On 10 May 1996 Beck Weathers, a pathologist from Dallas, was climbing Mount Everest with Rob Hall's expedition when he found he could no longer see well enough to go on. He waited high on the mountain for most of the day. On the way down a blizzard caught his group, and they lost their way close to the tents of the high camp. Rescuers who reached them in the night judged him beyond help. The next morning a doctor from his team found him still breathing under a crust of ice and, with nothing that could be done for him there, had to leave him as well; his family was told he was dead. By his own account he was unconscious for about fifteen hours. That afternoon he woke with his right hand frozen solid, stood up and walked into camp. He was not expected to live through the night, and did. He was helped down to a lower camp, and an army pilot, Lt. Col. Madan K.C., flew one of the highest helicopter rescues made up to that time to lift him off the mountain. He lost his right hand and part of the forearm, the fingers of his left hand, parts of both feet and his nose, which surgeons rebuilt. He went home to his family and wrote a book about it, Left for Dead. Other climbers caught in the same storm did not come back. Rook didn't believe it either.

Animated reconstruction of a true story. The mountain, camps, tent, helicopter and house in the film are generic low-poly sets, not models of the real places or aircraft; the other climbers are anonymous figures, and the cards on the case board are drawings made for the film. Sources give different lengths for the time he lay in the snow (fifteen to eighteen hours); the film uses his own figure.
source_notes: Read for this run (fetched 15 Nov 2026): Wikipedia ('Beck Weathers'); PBS NOVA Online, Audrey Salkeld's report from Base Camp dated 16 May 1996 (five days after the events); The Irish Times, 'Rebirth on the summit' (feature on his book, 1 July 2000); The Washington Post, live online discussion with Beck Weathers (11 May 2000, his own words); PBS Frontline, 'Storm Over Everest: the hour-by-hour unfolding disaster' (only the first part, up to the afternoon of 10 May, could be read in full); All That's Interesting (2021, updated 2024). Britannica, History.com, D Magazine and two further Frontline pages could not be fetched in this run, so nothing rests on them. Every narrated fact is in at least two of the pages read. 1996, Everest, a pathologist: Wikipedia, NOVA, Irish Times, ATI. From Dallas: Wikipedia, Washington Post, Irish Times. He could no longer see and stopped: Wikipedia (blinded by the effects of altitude after eye surgery), NOVA ('difficulty seeing'), Frontline (his own words), Irish Times, ATI. He waited: Wikipedia, NOVA, Frontline (ATI says the leader ordered him to stay, Wikipedia and Frontline that he chose to wait for the leader's return; the narration only says he stops and waits). Blizzard on the way down, the group lost close to camp: Wikipedia ('could not find Camp IV'), NOVA, Irish Times. Rescuers judged him beyond help: Irish Times ('left to die') and ATI ('deemed Weathers beyond help'); Wikipedia describes the same night. Next morning a doctor found him still breathing and had to leave him: Irish Times (cardiologist Stuart Hutchison 'had no choice but to leave them there'), ATI ('a Canadian doctor'), Wikipedia; NOVA reports that his death was 'confirmed by a doctor on the Col'. A second climber, Yasuko Namba, lay beside him and did not survive; the film does not show her. His wife was told he was dead: Irish Times, ATI (Washington Post: 'reported dead'). Fifteen hours: his own figure in the Washington Post discussion ('unconscious for about fifteen hours out of the 22 hours I was in the storm') and the Irish Times ('after 15 hours'); NOVA says sixteen and ATI and the Post's introduction eighteen, which is why the description gives the range. Woke that afternoon: NOVA (mid-afternoon), ATI (around 4 p.m.). Right hand frozen solid: Irish Times ('gloveless and frozen rock-solid'), ATI, NOVA ('hands and arms frozen to the elbows'). Stood up and walked into camp: all. Expected to die that night and did not: Wikipedia ('only tried to make him comfortable until he died'), Irish Times ('left him there to die too'). One of the highest helicopter rescues ever flown: NOVA ('one of the highest aerial rescues ever', from above the Icefall at about 20,000 ft, pilot Lt. Colonel Madan K.C.), Wikipedia ('the highest-altitude medical evacuation ever performed by helicopter up until that time'), Irish Times, ATI; the film gives no altitude because only one page read gives a figure. The Irish Times calls the pilot a Taiwanese army colonel; that conflicts with the usual account that he was a Nepalese army pilot, which none of the pages read states outright (NOVA, written that week, says an army helicopter and names a Taiwanese climber as the other man flown out), so the description only says 'an army pilot'. Lost his right hand (the arm was amputated between elbow and wrist), the fingers of his left hand and his nose: Wikipedia, ATI, Irish Times (right arm below the elbow, nose rebuilt). Wikipedia says the left thumb was lost as well and the Irish Times that half of it remains, so the narration says 'the fingers' and the drawn left hand keeps its thumb. Parts of both feet (Wikipedia, ATI) are in the description only. Conflict left out of the film: the number of deaths in the storm is given as eight or nine depending on the page and on what is counted, so no number is stated. Left out for length: the vision of his family that he says made him get up (one page read reports it), Rob Hall's death, the descent on foot to the lower camp, and his book.
